questions.q: List the supporting personified figures in Milton's "On Time" and briefly state what each represents.
questions.a: Correct answer: The "lazy leaden-stepping hours" (slow, heavy passage of time), the "heavy Plummets pace" (mechanical, leaden clock movement), "Eternity" (timeless divine realm), "Joy" (divine bliss), "Truth," "Peace," and "Love" (eternal virtues), "Death" and "Chance" (mortal adversaries). A wrong answer that lists only "Time" or misses the virtues reveals the student is still hunting for human characters instead of recognizing Milton's allegorical personifications. A wrong answer that calls the Hours "fast" shows misreading of "leaden-stepping" and "Plummets pace" — the student hasn't visualized the heavy clock weight.

questions.q: In "On Shakespeare," Milton calls the pyramid and stones "weak witness of thy name." Explain why the poet considers stone monuments weak compared to Shakespeare's "live-long Monument."
questions.a: Correct answer: Stone monuments decay and are passive; they only mark a body. Shakespeare's "live-long Monument" is his poetry, which actively lives in readers' minds ("each heart / Hath from the leaves of thy unvalu'd Book / Those Delphic lines with deep impression took"). It transforms readers ("make us Marble with too much conceaving") and outlasts pyramids. A wrong answer that says "stones break but poems don't" misses the active, psychological power of the "live-long Monument" — it doesn't just survive, it *possesses* the imagination. A wrong answer focusing only on the pyramid's size misses the contrast between external commemoration and internal transformation.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "foil" to the relationship between Time and the "leaden-stepping hours" in "On Time." How do the Hours intensify the portrayal of Time?
questions.a: Correct answer: The Hours are Time's instruments, yet their "leaden-stepping" slowness and the "Plummets pace" make Time's greed ("glut thy self") more monstrous — he devours even the slow, heavy mechanism that measures him. They are his unwilling accomplices, emphasizing his tyranny over the very tool that tracks him. Steps: 1) Identify Hours as Time's measuring tool. 2) Note their slowness ("leaden-stepping," "heavy Plummets"). 3) Contrast with Time's "envious," "greedy" speed. 4) Conclude: the foil highlights Time's hypocrisy — he rushes to consume what moves slowly. A wrong answer that says "Hours are part of Time" misses the dramatic tension; a wrong answer that calls Hours "fast" misreads "leaden."

questions.q: Compare the function of "Eternity" in "On Time" with the function of "Fame" in "On Shakespeare." How does each serve as a thematic resolution for its poem?
questions.a: Correct answer: Eternity is the *destination* — the final state where Time is consumed and the soul arrives ("long Eternity shall greet our bliss / With an individual kiss"). Fame is the *mechanism* — the living transmission of Shakespeare's work through readers ("great heir of Fame," "live-long Monument"). Eternity ends the poem vertically (transcendence); Fame extends it horizontally (posterity). Both resolve the conflict: Eternity by defeating Time, Fame by making stone monuments irrelevant. A wrong answer that treats both as "rewards" misses the structural difference: one is a metaphysical arrival, the other a cultural process. A wrong answer that says "Fame is for Shakespeare, Eternity is for us" ignores that the poem's "our bliss" includes the reader.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The Kings in 'On Shakespeare' are the most important supporting characters because they prove Shakespeare's greatness." Defend or refute with evidence.
questions.a: Correct answer: Refute. The Kings are a *concluding flourish*, not the core support. The real thematic work is done by "slow endeavouring art" (the foil to Shakespeare's ease), "Fancy" and "Memory" (the internal faculties Shakespeare activates), and "Fame" (the living monument). The Kings merely *wish* for his tomb — they are awestruck spectators, not active participants. Evidence: the poem spends 8 lines on the living monument's effect on readers ("each heart," "our fancy," "us Marble") and only 2 lines on Kings. A wrong answer that agrees reveals a "status-equals-significance" bias — assuming royal endorsement validates art, which is exactly the superficiality Milton critiques by making the *poet's* tomb the one Kings envy.

questions.q: Write a 4-line stanza in Milton's style where a new supporting character (e.g., "Silence," "Oblivion," "Criticism") confronts the protagonist of either poem. Use personification and one classical allusion.
questions.a: Criteria for a good answer: 1) Clear personification with capitalized name. 2) Confrontation with Time or Shakespeare. 3) Miltonic diction (inversion, Latinate vocabulary). 4) One classical allusion (e.g., Lethe, Muses, Cronos). 5) Thematic consistency. Example: "Hush, pale Oblivion, with thy Lethean wave, / Thy poppy'd wings o'er genius' grave; / But Shakespeare's voice, th' immortal Nine inspire, / Defies thy shade, and tunes the eternal lyre." A poor answer uses modern slang, lacks personification, or has no classical reference — showing the student hasn't internalized Milton's allegorical mode.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Supporting characters in poetry are personified ______, symbolic figures, or foils that interact with the protagonist to develop the poem's central conflict and theme.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're watching a play where the main actor (Time or Shakespeare) dominates the stage, but the supporting cast — the Hours dragging their feet, Eternity waiting with a kiss, the jealous "slow ______ art," the kings wishing for a poet's tomb — deliver lines that completely change the meaning of the lead's performance.
What is Supporting characters in poetry? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Supporting characters in poetry are personified abstractions, symbolic figures, or foils that interact with the protagonist to develop the poem's central conflict and theme.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Supporting characters in poetry?
questions.a: Students think "supporting characters" must be human figures with dialogue.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently identify all supporting personifications in both poems, explain how each functions as a foil or thematic counterpoint to the protagonist (Time/Shakespeare), and write a structured PEEL paragraph analyzing one supporting figure's contribution to the poem's argument about mortality or artistic immortality.
